Biodiversity Conservation

Biodiversity Conservation is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Biodiversity Conservation
Why variety on and around the farm is productive rather than decorative.

Biodiversity on a farm is not an ornament; it is infrastructure. Pollinators set fruit. Predatory insects and birds suppress pests. Soil organisms cycle nutrients. Diverse crop varieties spread risk across different tolerances. Each of these is a service the farm would otherwise have to buy or do without.

Monoculture removes these services and replaces them with purchased inputs. That can work while the inputs are affordable and effective, but it makes the system brittle: one resistant pest or one price rise and there is no fallback.

Key points

  • Maintain flowering plants and hedgerows to shelter pollinators and predators through the year.
  • Grow more than one variety of the main crop so a disease cannot take everything.
  • Retain trees on and around fields for shade, roots, habitat and firewood.
  • Avoid broad-spectrum pesticides, which remove beneficial organisms with the target.
  • Preserve local landraces — they carry tolerance traits bred over generations for these conditions.

Example

A district plants a single high-yielding cassava variety everywhere. When a mosaic disease strain arrives that this variety cannot resist, losses are severe and uniform. Neighbouring communities growing three varieties lose one and keep two.

Why this matters

Genetic and ecological diversity is the cheapest insurance a farming system has, and it is lost quietly through decisions that each look sensible on their own. Recognising the value of what is being replaced is part of giving sound advice.

2. Measure

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Environmental Stewardship

Environmental Stewardship is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Environmental Stewardship
The farmer's responsibility beyond the farm boundary.

Environmental stewardship is managing a farm with regard for effects that fall outside its boundary: water quality downstream, soil that leaves the field, chemicals that drift or leach, and habitat that the farm shares with its neighbours.

These effects are real costs, simply borne by someone else. A farm that loses fertiliser to a stream has paid for input it did not use and imposed a problem on everyone downstream. Stewardship and good management usually point the same way, which is what makes it practical rather than merely virtuous.

Key points

  • Keep buffer strips of vegetation between cultivated land and watercourses.
  • Apply chemicals at the labelled rate, in the right conditions, and never near open water.
  • Dispose of containers and expired products properly; never reuse pesticide containers.
  • Protect the recharge area around wells and springs from contamination.
  • Keep records of what was applied where and when — this is both good practice and increasingly required.

Example

A farm applies fertiliser immediately before heavy rain. Much of it washes into the creek that supplies the village downstream, causing algal growth. The farm paid for nutrients that never reached the crop and damaged a shared resource with the same act.

Why this matters

Buyers, certification schemes and lenders increasingly ask for evidence of environmental practice, and regulators are becoming more active. Beyond compliance, stewardship is usually just efficiency seen from outside the fence.

lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle

1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Farm Planning

Farm Planning is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Farm Planning
Deciding what to grow where, before the season starts.

Farm planning allocates the farm's limited resources — land, labour, cash and time — across enterprises for the coming season. It answers four questions: what to produce, on which plots, when, and with what inputs.

The binding constraint is rarely land. On most smallholdings it is labour during the peak weeding period, or cash at planting time. A plan that looks excellent on paper fails if it requires forty person-days in a fortnight when only fifteen are available.

Key points

  • Start from the constraint, not from the wish list — identify what runs out first.
  • Draw a labour calendar by month; peaks that exceed available labour must be redesigned.
  • Stagger planting dates to spread both labour demand and market risk.
  • Match crops to plots by soil, drainage and distance from water and from home.
  • Plan the cash flow alongside the activities; inputs are needed before revenue arrives.

Example

A farmer plans three hectares of maize and one of vegetables. The labour calendar shows both need weeding in the same three weeks. Shifting the vegetables two weeks later separates the peaks and makes the whole plan feasible with the household's own labour.

Why this matters

Planning is where most of the value in farm management is created, because it is the point at which problems are cheap to fix. Being able to build a labour calendar and a cash-flow plan is a concrete, employable skill in cooperative and project work.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Resource Management

Resource Management is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Resource Management
Getting the most from land, water, labour, cash and equipment.

Resource management asks a single question of every resource: what is the return on the next unit of it? Land, water, labour, cash and equipment each produce diminishing returns, and the skill is directing each one to where it earns most.

This is why the same input can be right on one farm and wrong on another. Fertiliser on a farm short of water earns little; the same money spent on a water tank might earn a great deal. Managing resources means comparing the alternatives, not evaluating each in isolation.

Key points

  • Identify the scarcest resource first; it sets the value of everything else.
  • Compare returns per unit of the scarce resource, not per hectare, when labour or cash is binding.
  • Shared or hired equipment is often better than owned equipment used a few days a year.
  • Track use, not just purchase — fuel bought is not fuel usefully used.
  • Resources have timing: cash in March and cash in September are not the same resource.

Example

A farmer can spend her remaining cash on fertiliser or on hiring labour for timely weeding. On her farm weeds are the bigger yield thief, so the same money returns more through labour. Evaluating fertiliser alone would have missed that.

Why this matters

This comparative habit is what distinguishes management from activity. It is also directly relevant to advisory work, where the useful question is never is this a good input but is this the best use of the farmer's next dollar.

lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle

1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Farm Budgeting

Farm Budgeting is an agribusiness concept used to understand customers, costs, income, risk, value, and business decisions.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Farm Budgeting
Working out in advance whether an enterprise will make money.

A farm budget estimates the revenue and costs of an enterprise before it is undertaken. The standard tool is the gross margin: revenue minus variable costs, calculated per hectare or per animal.

Variable costs change with the size of the enterprise — seed, fertiliser, casual labour, harvesting, transport. Fixed costs do not — land rent, permanent staff, equipment depreciation. Gross margin deliberately excludes fixed costs so that enterprises can be compared with each other on equal terms.

Key points

  • Gross margin = revenue − variable costs, always stated per unit (per hectare, per animal).
  • Use realistic yields, not best-ever yields; budget on what you actually achieved last time.
  • Value family labour, even if unpaid — otherwise every enterprise looks profitable.
  • Test the budget against a low price and a low yield, not only the expected case.
  • The enterprise with the highest gross margin per hectare may not be best if labour, not land, is scarce.

Example

A farmer budgets one hectare of maize: expected yield 2.5 tonnes at $300 per tonne gives revenue of $750. Seed, fertiliser, ploughing, weeding labour and transport total $430. The gross margin is $320 per hectare. At a low yield of 1.8 tonnes the margin falls to $110 — still positive, so the enterprise survives a poor season.

Why this matters

Budgeting is how a proposal, a loan application or a business plan is judged. It is also the discipline that stops an attractive-sounding enterprise from being started on optimism. Every module from here on assumes you can build one.

questions.explanation: Gross margin subtracts only variable costs, which allows enterprises to be compared fairly.

questions.question: Why should unpaid family labour still be valued in a budget?

lessons.html:

🌱 Record Keeping
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Record Keeping

Record Keeping is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Record Keeping
What to write down, and the design that makes records survive.

Farm records are the raw material of every analysis in this course. The problem is almost never that farmers cannot analyse; it is that the records were never kept, or were kept in a form that cannot be used.

A usable record has four elements: what happened, where (which plot), when (the date), and how much (quantity and cost). Miss any one and the record loses most of its value.

Key points

  • Record at the moment, not at the end of the week — memory reconstructs, and reconstruction is invention.
  • Use one line per event, never a running total that overwrites.
  • Keep the categories few and fixed; a system with thirty categories will not be maintained.
  • Record the unusual too: the dry spell, the pest outbreak, the late delivery. These explain the numbers later.
  • Whoever does the work should do the recording, on paper or phone, in the field.

Example

Two farmers both keep books. The first writes fertiliser $80. The second writes 12 May, Plot B, 50kg NPK, $80, applied before rain. A year later the first has an expense; the second can explain a yield, compare plots, and judge whether the timing was right.

Why this matters

Designing a record system that people will actually maintain is among the most valuable things you can do for a farm or a cooperative, and it is a common job requirement. The hard part is not the format; it is keeping it simple enough to survive a busy week.

Tap a word to open its definition.

Farm Productivity

Farm Productivity is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Farm Productivity
Measuring output properly, and the denominators that matter.

Productivity is output divided by input. The trap is choosing only one denominator. Yield per hectare is the familiar measure, but it answers only the question of how well land is used — and land is often not the scarce resource.

A farm should track productivity against each scarce resource: output per hectare, output per labour day, output per dollar of variable cost, and for livestock, output per animal. The picture that emerges is frequently different from the yield figure alone.

Key points

  • Land productivity — tonnes per hectare; matters where land is limited.
  • Labour productivity — output per person-day; matters where labour binds.
  • Capital productivity — return per dollar spent; matters where cash binds.
  • Partial measures can disagree, and the disagreement is informative.
  • Compare against your own past performance before comparing against anyone else's.

Example

A farmer raises yield from 2.0 to 2.4 tonnes per hectare by weeding three times instead of twice. Land productivity improved by 20 percent, but the extra labour cut output per person-day. If labour is her scarce resource, she has made the farm worse, not better.

Why this matters

This is the analytical core of farm assessment. Being able to compute several productivity measures and explain why they disagree is exactly the sort of reasoning that distinguishes a competent analyst from someone quoting a yield figure.

lessons.title: 5.6 Labor Management
lessons.html:

🌱 Labor Management
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Labor Management

Labor Management is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Labor Management
Organising the people who do the work, at the times it must be done.

Agricultural labour is unlike most other work: it is seasonal, weather-dependent, and much of it must happen within a narrow window or the value is lost. Weeding done three weeks late is not partially useful; it is largely wasted.

Labour management therefore means planning for peaks, not for averages. The annual labour requirement may be modest while the three critical weeks are impossible.

Key points

  • Map labour demand by task and week; the peaks are where the plan succeeds or fails.
  • Reduce peaks by staggering planting or choosing varieties with different maturity dates.
  • Agree terms clearly with hired labour — rate, task, measure and payment date — before work starts.
  • Task rates (per row, per bag) suit measurable work; daily rates suit work needing care.
  • Supervise quality on task-rate work; speed and care pull against each other.

Example

A farmer hires weeders on a task rate per row and returns to find the rows cleared quickly but shallowly, with roots left to regrow. The rate encouraged exactly what it measured. A daily rate with supervision, or a task rate with an inspection standard, would have produced better weeding.

Why this matters

Labour is usually the largest single cost on a smallholding and the most common cause of a good plan failing. Understanding how payment terms shape behaviour is practical management knowledge that applies well beyond farming.

questions.question: Why must labour planning focus on peaks rather than annual totals?

lessons.title: 5.7 Farm Safety
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Farm Safety
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Farm Safety

Farm Safety is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Farm Safety
The hazards that actually injure people, and how to control them.

Farms are among the more dangerous workplaces anywhere. The recurring hazards are machinery, chemicals, animals, heights and falls, heat and tools. Most injuries are foreseeable and follow the same few patterns.

Safety is best handled by controlling the hazard rather than relying on care. Guarding a moving part protects everyone permanently; telling people to be careful protects them only while they are paying attention.

Key points

  • Keep guards on rotating machinery; power take-off shafts cause severe injuries.
  • Store agrochemicals locked, labelled and away from food; never decant into drink bottles.
  • Use protective equipment when spraying — gloves, eye protection and a mask suited to the product.
  • Never work under a raised implement supported only by hydraulics.
  • Handle livestock with an escape route in mind; large animals injure by crushing more than by attack.
  • Keep a first-aid kit and make sure someone knows where it is.

Example

A worker decants herbicide into an old soft-drink bottle to carry it to the field. It is later picked up and drunk by a child. Almost every element of this is preventable by one rule: chemicals stay in labelled containers, locked away.

Why this matters

Beyond the human cost, an injury on a smallholding removes the labour the household depends on at exactly the moment it is needed. Safety knowledge is also a standard requirement in any supervisory or certification role.

lessons.title: 5.8 Agricultural Risk Management
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Agricultural Risk Management
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Agricultural Risk Management

Agricultural Risk Management is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Agricultural Risk Management
Identifying what can go wrong, and deciding what to do about each risk.

Farming carries five main risk types: production (weather, pests, disease), price (markets move), financial (credit, interest, cash flow), institutional (policy, regulation) and personal (illness, injury, death of a key worker).

For each risk there are four possible responses: avoid it, reduce it, transfer it (insurance, contracts) or accept it. Accepting is a legitimate choice when the cost of the alternatives exceeds the expected loss — but it should be a decision, not an oversight.

Key points

  • Assess each risk by likelihood and by severity; treat the severe ones first even if they are unlikely.
  • Diversification reduces production and price risk together.
  • Contracts transfer price risk; index insurance can transfer weather risk where it is available.
  • Keeping a cash or grain reserve is the simplest and most reliable buffer.
  • The most dangerous risks are the severe, uninsured ones nobody has named.

Example

A farmer with one crop and one buyer faces production and price risk concentrated in a single point of failure. Adding a second crop with a different harvest window, and a second buyer, addresses both without any new technology or spending.

Why this matters

Risk management is what banks and investors examine most closely in agricultural lending, and it is what separates a business plan that is credible from one that is optimistic. Naming risks explicitly is half the work.

lessons.title: 5.9 Farm Performance Evaluation
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Farm Performance Evaluation
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Farm Performance Evaluation

Farm Performance Evaluation is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Farm Performance Evaluation
Judging how the farm actually did, honestly.

Performance evaluation compares what happened against what was planned, and asks why they differ. It happens after the season and it is where learning either occurs or does not.

An honest evaluation separates three causes of a shortfall: things outside the farm's control (weather, market prices), things inside its control that were done poorly (late weeding, wrong spacing), and things that were planned wrongly in the first place. Blaming the weather for everything prevents improvement; blaming yourself for the weather is equally useless.

Key points

  • Compare planned versus actual for yield, cost, labour and revenue — not yield alone.
  • Compute gross margin per hectare and per labour day for each enterprise.
  • Rank enterprises; the weakest is a candidate for change or removal.
  • Separate controllable from uncontrollable causes explicitly.
  • Write down three specific changes for next season, with the evidence for each.

Example

A season is evaluated. Maize underperformed, and the immediate explanation is poor rainfall. But the records show weeding happened three weeks after planting instead of two, and the plot weeded on time yielded 30 percent more than the one that was late, under the same rain. The weather was real; it was not the whole story.

Why this matters

This is the step that turns a season of records into improvement, and it is the substance of the capstone. It is also what an employer means when they ask whether you can evaluate a programme rather than merely report on one.

4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Farm Business Planning

Farm Business Planning is an agribusiness concept used to understand customers, costs, income, risk, value, and business decisions.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Farm Business Planning
Writing the document that turns a farm into a fundable business.

A farm business plan sets out what the business does, what it intends to achieve, how it will do it, and what it needs. It is written for a reader — a lender, an investor, a partner or the farmer themselves — and its job is to let that reader judge whether the plan is sound.

The section that decides most applications is the financial one. Everything else can be well written and the plan still fails if the numbers do not hold together or rest on yields the farm has never achieved.

Key points

  • Summary — what the business does and what it is asking for, in one page.
  • The business — location, land, enterprises, people and current performance.
  • Market — who buys, at what price, and why they will buy from you.
  • Operations — the production plan, calendar and inputs.
  • Financials — gross margins, cash flow by month, and the funding requirement.
  • Risks — the main ones named, with the response to each.

Example

A plan requests a loan for irrigation equipment. The monthly cash flow shows the loan drawn in February, equipment installed in March, and the first additional revenue in August — with the repayment schedule starting in April. The gap is visible, and it is exactly what the lender needs to see and discuss.

Why this matters

This document is how agricultural finance is accessed, and writing one competently is a service you can offer immediately. It also forces every earlier skill in this module — budgeting, planning, risk, evaluation — into one coherent statement.

lessons.title: 6.1 GPS in Agriculture
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 GPS in Agriculture
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

GPS in Agriculture

GPS in Agriculture is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 GPS in Agriculture
Knowing exactly where you are, and what that makes possible.

GPS receives timing signals from satellites and computes a position on the ground. A phone gives roughly 3 to 10 metres of accuracy, which is enough to map plot boundaries, mark a sampling point or record where a problem was seen. Survey-grade equipment reaches centimetres, which is what guided machinery needs.

For smallholder work, phone-grade accuracy is almost always sufficient. The value is not precision for its own sake; it is that a location can be recorded, returned to, and linked to other data.

Key points

  • Accuracy improves with a clear view of the sky; tree canopy and buildings degrade it.
  • Record a boundary by walking the perimeter and capturing points at each corner.
  • Always note the date with a position — boundaries and features change.
  • A waypoint is a single point; a track is a recorded path; a polygon encloses an area.
  • Coordinates are useless without knowing which system they are in — note it.

Example

A field officer marks the location of every plot where she takes a soil sample. Two seasons later the laboratory results, the yields and the positions can be joined together, and a map shows that the low-phosphorus samples all lie along one side of the farm.

Why this matters

Location is the key that joins otherwise separate records. Soil results, yield figures, pest sightings and photographs become far more useful when each carries a position, and that joining is the foundation of everything in this module.

lessons.title: 6.2 Geographic Information Systems (GIS)
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Geographic Information Systems (GIS)
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Geographic Information Systems (GIS)

Geographic Information Systems (GIS) is a digital-agriculture concept used to collect, interpret, communicate, or act on farm information.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Geographic Information Systems (GIS)
Storing, combining and analysing information that has a location.

A GIS holds data in layers, each layer describing one thing across the same area: plot boundaries, soil types, elevation, water sources, roads, yield. Because every layer shares a coordinate system, they can be laid over one another and questions asked that span them.

That overlay is the point. Any single layer is a map. Several layers together answer questions like which plots are on sandy soil, more than 500 metres from water, and yielded below average last season.

Key points

  • Vector data represents points, lines and polygons — a well, a track, a field.
  • Raster data represents a grid of cells — satellite imagery, elevation models.
  • Attributes are the information attached to each feature: a plot's area, crop and owner.
  • Layers must share a coordinate reference system or they will not align.
  • Free tools such as QGIS do everything a farm-scale analysis needs.

Example

Overlaying a yield map on a soil map reveals that the low-yielding corner of a field corresponds exactly to a patch of shallow soil over rock. The recommendation is not more fertiliser; it is to accept lower expectations there, or use it for a less demanding crop.

Why this matters

GIS is a named requirement in a large share of AgriTech and development job adverts, and QGIS is free. Being able to build a simple layered farm map is a demonstrable skill that fits directly into your capstone portfolio.

lessons.title: 6.3 Remote Sensing
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Remote Sensing
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Remote Sensing

collecting information about land or crops from a distance using sensors on satellites, aircraft, or drones

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Remote Sensing
Measuring crops from a distance, and what the imagery actually shows.

Remote sensing measures reflected light from a distance — from satellites, aircraft or drones. Healthy vegetation reflects strongly in the near-infrared and absorbs red light for photosynthesis; stressed vegetation reflects less infrared. Comparing those bands produces a vegetation index, of which NDVI is the most widely used.

NDVI does not tell you what is wrong. It tells you where the crop differs from its surroundings. Diagnosis still requires going to the field, which is why remote sensing directs scouting rather than replacing it.

Key points

  • Free imagery from Sentinel-2 gives 10-metre pixels every few days — usable at field scale.
  • Cloud cover is the main limitation in humid tropical regions.
  • Compare the same field across dates; a single image has little meaning without a baseline.
  • Index values differ by crop and growth stage, so absolute thresholds transfer poorly.
  • Always ground-truth: visit the anomaly and find out what it is.

Example

An NDVI image shows a pale strip across a maize field. On the ground it turns out to be a buried pipeline where the soil was compacted during installation. The imagery found it in seconds; only the field visit explained it.

Why this matters

Free satellite imagery has made large-area crop monitoring accessible without any equipment purchase. Understanding what an index does and does not tell you prevents the common error of treating a colourful map as a diagnosis.

lessons.title: 6.4 Yield Monitoring
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Yield Monitoring
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Yield Monitoring

Yield Monitoring is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Yield Monitoring
Measuring output where it was produced, not just in total.

Yield monitoring records how much was harvested from each part of a field rather than only the total. On mechanised farms a sensor on the combine logs flow and position continuously. On a smallholding the same information comes from weighing each plot's harvest separately and recording it against the plot.

The method matters far less than the discipline. A yield map built from twelve weighed plots tells you almost as much about within-field variation as a machine-generated one, and it costs a scale and a notebook.

Key points

  • Weigh by plot, not by farm; a single total cannot show variation.
  • Record moisture if you can — wet and dry grain are not comparable weights.
  • Keep plot areas accurate, since yield is weight divided by area.
  • One season of yield data identifies patterns; several confirm whether they are stable.
  • Stable low-yielding areas are worth investigating; variable ones usually reflect weather.

Example

A farmer weighs the harvest from each of her eight beds separately for the first time. Two beds consistently produce a third less. Investigating those two reveals a hardpan layer from years of hoeing to the same depth, which deeper loosening then corrects.

Why this matters

Yield data is the outcome measure against which every other decision is judged. Without it, the effect of a change in variety, fertiliser or timing can only be guessed at, and the whole feedback loop of smart farming cannot close.

lessons.title: 6.5 Variable Rate Technology
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Variable Rate Technology
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Variable Rate Technology

Variable Rate Technology is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Variable Rate Technology
Applying different amounts in different places, and when it pays.

Variable rate technology applies inputs at rates that change across a field according to a prescription map. Machinery-based systems adjust automatically by GPS position. Manual variable rate — applying more to a known poor zone and less to a rich one — achieves the same principle with a bucket and knowledge.

The economics depend on three things: how much the field actually varies, how expensive the input is, and how accurately you can map the variation. If a field is uniform, variable rate saves nothing and costs effort.

Key points

  • A prescription map divides the field into zones with a rate for each.
  • Build zones from stable factors — soil type, depth, historic yield — not from a single season.
  • Higher input cost strengthens the case; cheap inputs rarely justify the effort.
  • Rates can go up in poor zones (to correct) or down (to avoid waste) — both are legitimate strategies.
  • Two or three zones capture most of the benefit; more adds complexity faster than value.

Example

A farmer splits a field into a fertile low section and a sandy rise. She applies less nitrogen to the low section, which was already lodging from excess, and more to the rise. Total fertiliser is unchanged, lodging drops and yield rises. The gain came from redistribution alone.

Why this matters

Variable rate is where precision agriculture pays or fails commercially. Being able to judge whether a field varies enough to justify it, and to build simple zones from existing knowledge, is more valuable than being able to operate the machinery.

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Precision Irrigation
Watering according to what the crop and soil actually need.

Precision irrigation applies water in the right amount, at the right time, in the right place. It requires knowing three things: how much water the soil currently holds, how much the crop is using, and how much the system delivers per hour.

Soil moisture can be measured with sensors or judged by feel and appearance at depth. Crop use is estimated from evapotranspiration, which rises with temperature, sunshine and wind. System output is measured once by catching and timing the flow.

Key points

  • Irrigate to refill the root zone to field capacity, no further.
  • Deficit irrigation deliberately applies less than full demand, accepting a small yield loss for a large water saving — useful when water, not land, is scarce.
  • Scheduling by soil moisture beats scheduling by calendar every time.
  • Know your system's delivery rate; without it, run time cannot be converted to depth applied.
  • Check for blockages and leaks regularly, especially in drip lines.

Example

A grower measures that her drip system delivers 4mm per hour to the bed area. Her sensor shows the root zone is 20mm short of field capacity. She runs the system for five hours rather than guessing, and checks the sensor afterwards to confirm.

Why this matters

Water is usually the most valuable input a farm has, and irrigation is where the largest quantities are wasted through simple ignorance of how much is being applied. Converting run time into depth applied is a small calculation with a large effect.

lessons.title: 6.7 Soil Mapping
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Soil Mapping
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Soil Mapping

Soil Mapping is an agronomy practice or measure used to understand and improve soil conditions and crop nutrition.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Soil Mapping
Recording how soil varies across a farm, and using it.

Soil mapping records how soil properties vary spatially. It combines what can be observed directly — texture by feel, depth by auger, colour, stoniness — with laboratory analysis of samples and, where available, existing soil survey maps.

The critical discipline is sampling. A sample must represent the zone it is taken from, which means combining several sub-samples from across the zone rather than taking one scoop. Where the sample came from must be recorded, or the result cannot be mapped.

Key points

  • Divide the farm into zones that look different, then sample each zone separately.
  • Take 10 to 15 sub-samples per zone, mix them, and send a portion — this is a composite sample.
  • Sample to the depth roots occupy, usually 0–20cm for annual crops.
  • Avoid unusual spots — old cattle pens, ash heaps, headlands — unless mapping them deliberately.
  • Record GPS position, date and depth with every sample.

Example

A farm is sampled as one unit and returns a moderate average pH of 5.9. Sampled by zone, the same farm shows one area at 4.9 and another at 6.6. The average described neither and would have led to a lime recommendation that was wrong for both.

Why this matters

Soil is the most expensive thing to get wrong and the cheapest to measure properly. A zone-based soil map underpins variable rate application, explains yield variation, and is a strong component of a farm portfolio.

questions.question: What is a composite sample?
options: A sample split between two laboratories
One scoop taken from the field centre
Several sub-samples from across a zone mixed together
A sample taken at two depths
questions.explanation: Combining sub-samples makes the result represent the zone rather than one arbitrary point.

It may describe no part of the farm accurately

questions.question: To what depth are annual crops usually sampled?

lessons.title: 6.8 Precision Crop Management
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Precision Crop Management
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Precision Crop Management

Precision Crop Management is a crop-production concept used to plan, monitor, protect, harvest, or evaluate a farm enterprise.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Precision Crop Management
Bringing the tools together into a season-long management plan.

Precision crop management is the integration of everything in this module: mapping the variation, defining zones, planning differentiated treatment, monitoring the response and recording the result. It is a cycle rather than a purchase.

The season runs: before planting, define zones from soil and yield history; at planting, vary seed rate and variety by zone; during the season, monitor by scouting and imagery and apply nutrients and protection where needed; at harvest, measure yield by zone and update the maps.

Key points

  • Start with the zones you are most confident about; refine them over seasons.
  • Not every input needs to vary — choose the one or two with the largest cost or response.
  • Scouting on the ground remains essential; imagery directs it but does not replace it.
  • Close the loop: this season's yield map is next season's zone map.
  • Keep records against zones so the effect of differentiated treatment can be measured.

Example

Over three seasons a farmer refines her field into three zones. Seed rate is raised in the strong zone and lowered in the weak one, nitrogen is redistributed, and yield variation across the field narrows while total input spend stays flat. No new machinery was bought.

Why this matters

This is the practical form precision agriculture takes on a smallholding, and it is what your capstone will demonstrate. It shows an employer that you understand precision agriculture as a management discipline rather than as a category of equipment.

lessons.html:

1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Precision Livestock Farming

Precision Livestock Farming is a livestock or aquaculture concept used to support welfare, health, production, records, and responsible management.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Precision Livestock Farming
Managing animals individually rather than as a herd.

Precision livestock farming applies the same principle to animals: measure the individual rather than the group. Identification is the foundation — ear tags, and increasingly electronic tags or collars — because without knowing which animal is which, nothing can be attributed.

What is measured varies with the system: weight gain, milk yield, feed intake, activity, body temperature, and location. Activity monitoring is widely used to detect oestrus and to flag illness early, since a sick animal usually moves differently before it looks unwell.

Key points

  • Identify every animal individually; this is the prerequisite for everything else.
  • Weigh regularly — growth rate reveals problems long before condition looks poor.
  • Individual records expose the poor performers hidden inside a herd average.
  • Early illness detection is worth more than treatment, because treatment starts sooner.
  • Simple systems work: a tag, a scale and a notebook deliver most of the benefit.

Example

A dairy herd averages an acceptable yield. Individual records show that three of the twenty cows produce so little that they cost more to feed than they return. Culling those three raises the herd average and cuts feed cost, and neither would have been visible from the bulk tank.

Why this matters

Herd averages hide both the best and the worst animals. Individual measurement is where livestock profitability is found, and setting up a workable animal recording system is directly employable with dairy, poultry and cooperative operations.

lessons.html:

1. Observe
2. Measure

4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Precision Agriculture Project

Precision Agriculture Project is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Precision Agriculture Project
Build a zone map for one real field and a differentiated plan.

This project asks you to apply the module to a single real field. You will map it, divide it into zones on evidence, and produce a treatment plan that differs by zone with the reasoning stated.

Choose a field you can walk. It does not need to be large — half a hectare with genuine variation is better than ten hectares you cannot inspect.

Key points

  • Map the field — walk the boundary with a phone GPS and record the area.
  • Observe variation — walk the field and note where soil, colour, drainage, crop vigour or weeds differ. Photograph and record positions.
  • Sample — take a composite soil sample from each apparent zone, recording position and depth.
  • Define zones — two or three, each with a short justification.
  • Plan treatment — state what you would apply differently in each zone and why.
  • Estimate the effect — what you expect to change, and how you would measure whether it did.
  • Present — a zone map, a table of zone characteristics, and one page of recommendations.

Example

A strong submission might identify a wet lower zone, a mid-slope zone and a dry stony rise; recommend drainage and a later planting date on the wet zone, standard treatment in the middle, and a shorter-duration variety with reduced nitrogen on the rise; and specify weighing each zone's harvest separately to test whether it worked.

Why this matters

This project is the core precision agriculture evidence in your portfolio. It demonstrates the full chain — observation, measurement, zoning, differentiated action, and a plan to verify — which is exactly what a precision agriculture role consists of.

lessons.title: 7.1 Introduction to IoT
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Introduction to IoT
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Introduction to IoT

Introduction to IoT is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Introduction to IoT
Devices that sense and report on their own, and what that requires.

The Internet of Things means physical devices that measure something and send the result somewhere without a person taking the reading. On a farm that might be a soil probe, a weather station, a tank level float, a gate sensor or an animal collar.

Every IoT device has four parts: a sensor that measures, a processor that formats the reading, a radio that transmits it, and a power source. In rural deployment, power and connectivity fail far more often than sensors do.

Key points

  • Match the transmission technology to the distance and the data volume — most farm sensors send tiny messages rarely.
  • LoRaWAN and similar low-power networks reach kilometres on a battery; WiFi does not.
  • Solar with a battery is the usual power answer, sized for the worst week of cloud.
  • Devices must fail visibly — a sensor that silently stops is worse than none, because decisions continue on stale data.
  • Budget for maintenance: dust, humidity, insects, livestock and theft all take a toll.

Example

A farm installs five soil probes. Three months later two have stopped reporting, but the dashboard still shows their last values with no indication they are stale. Irrigation decisions are made on data from a sensor that has been dead for weeks.

Why this matters

IoT is where AgriTech projects most often fail expensively, and almost always for practical reasons — power, connectivity, maintenance — rather than technical ones. Knowing what to ask about deployment is worth more than knowing sensor specifications.

lessons.title: 7.2 Smart Sensors
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Smart Sensors
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Smart Sensors

Smart Sensors is a digital-agriculture concept used to collect, interpret, communicate, or act on farm information.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Smart Sensors
What can be measured on a farm, and how to trust the numbers.

A smart sensor measures a physical quantity and converts it to a digital value. Common agricultural sensors measure soil moisture and temperature, air temperature and humidity, rainfall, leaf wetness, light, water flow and level, and for livestock, movement and body temperature.

Every sensor has three properties you must know: accuracy (how close to the true value), precision (how repeatable) and drift (how the reading changes over time as the sensor ages). A sensor that drifts is worse than one that is simply inaccurate, because the error changes.

Key points

  • Calibrate against a known reference when installed, and check periodically.
  • Placement determines meaning — a temperature sensor in direct sun measures the sun, not the air.
  • Depth matters for soil sensors; readings at 10cm and 40cm answer different questions.
  • One sensor represents one point; variation across a field needs several or careful siting.
  • Record the sensor's location, depth and installation date alongside its readings.

Example

A moisture probe installed beside a drip emitter reads wet whenever irrigation runs, regardless of the rest of the bed. Moved to a representative position between emitters, the same probe starts producing readings that actually describe the root zone.

Why this matters

Sensor data is only as good as the placement and calibration behind it, and both are decisions made by a person. Being the person who knows why a reading is wrong is considerably more valuable than being the person who installs the device.

questions.question: Why is sensor drift worse than simple inaccuracy?
options: Because the error changes over time and cannot be corrected once
questions.explanation: A constant offset can be corrected; an error that changes cannot be, without recalibration.

questions.question: What does placement determine?
questions.explanation: A sensor measures its immediate surroundings, so siting defines what the number represents.

questions.question: What should be recorded alongside sensor readings?
questions.explanation: Without this context the readings cannot be interpreted or compared later.

lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Soil Moisture Sensors
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Soil Moisture Sensors

Soil Moisture Sensors is an agronomy practice or measure used to understand and improve soil conditions and crop nutrition.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Soil Moisture Sensors
Measuring water in the root zone, and reading the result correctly.

Soil moisture sensors estimate how much water the soil holds. Most affordable types measure the soil's electrical properties, which change with water content. The reading must be interpreted against two reference points: field capacity, the water the soil holds after drainage, and the wilting point, below which the plant cannot extract water.

The usable water is the gap between them, and that gap depends entirely on soil texture. Sandy soil holds little; clay holds much more but releases it less readily. The same percentage reading means different things in different soils.

Key points

  • Install at root-zone depth, and ideally at two depths to see whether water is reaching down.
  • Ensure firm soil contact — an air gap around the probe gives a falsely dry reading.
  • Interpret against field capacity and wilting point for that soil, not against a generic threshold.
  • Watch the trend rather than the absolute value; the rate of drying tells you when to irrigate.
  • Salinity and temperature affect electrical readings on cheaper sensors.

Example

A farmer sees 25 percent moisture and does not irrigate, assuming it is adequate. On her sandy soil, field capacity is 18 percent and wilting point is 8 percent — so 25 percent is saturated and she is at risk of waterlogging, not drought. The number was meaningless without the references.

Why this matters

Irrigation is the decision most commonly improved by sensors, and misreading moisture data is the commonest way to waste that investment. Understanding field capacity and wilting point turns a number into a decision.

questions.question: What two reference points give a moisture reading meaning?
questions.explanation: Usable water lies between these two points, and both depend on the soil.

questions.question: Why does an air gap around a probe cause a false reading?
options: It gives a falsely dry reading because contact with soil is lost
It causes the probe to over-read
questions.explanation: The sensor measures its immediate surroundings, and air reads as very dry.

questions.question: Why watch the trend rather than a single value?
options: The rate of drying indicates when irrigation will be needed
questions.explanation: How fast the soil is drying predicts the timing of the next irrigation, which a single reading cannot.

lessons.html:

1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Weather Stations

Weather Stations is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Weather Stations
Measuring conditions on the farm rather than at the airport.

A farm weather station records the conditions the crop is actually experiencing. The standard measurements are rainfall, air temperature, humidity, wind speed and direction, and solar radiation. From temperature and humidity you also get leaf wetness duration and evapotranspiration, which drive disease risk and irrigation demand.

On-farm measurement matters because rainfall in particular is intensely local. A station ten kilometres away can record a downpour that missed your field entirely, and irrigation decisions made on that figure will be wrong.

Key points

  • Site the rain gauge in the open, away from trees and buildings, at standard height.
  • Temperature sensors need a radiation shield or they read the sun, not the air.
  • A simple manual rain gauge read daily is far better than no rainfall record at all.
  • Accumulated temperature (growing degree days) predicts crop stage better than calendar days.
  • Historical records from your own station become the baseline that makes each season interpretable.

Example

Two farms four kilometres apart record 12mm and 47mm from the same storm. The farmer relying on the regional figure of 45mm skips irrigation and loses establishment on a newly planted field that received almost nothing.

Why this matters

Weather is the single largest source of variation in farming, and on-farm records are what let you separate weather effects from management effects when evaluating a season. Without them, every disappointing result can be blamed on the rain.

questions.question: Why does on-farm rainfall measurement matter?
options: Rainfall is intensely local and can differ greatly over a few kilometres
questions.explanation: Convective rainfall varies sharply over short distances, so distant figures can be badly wrong.

questions.question: What do temperature sensors need to read air temperature correctly?
questions.explanation: Without shielding the sensor is heated by direct sun and reports far above the true air temperature.

questions.question: What predicts crop development stage better than calendar days?
options: Accumulated temperature, or growing degree days
questions.explanation: Crops develop in response to accumulated heat, which varies between seasons at the same calendar date.

lessons.title: 7.5 Smart Irrigation Systems
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Smart Irrigation Systems
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Smart Irrigation Systems

Smart Irrigation Systems is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Smart Irrigation Systems
Irrigation that decides for itself when and how much to apply.

A smart irrigation system connects moisture or weather sensing to the valve that controls water. In its simplest form a moisture threshold opens a valve; in a fuller form the system uses evapotranspiration, forecast rainfall and soil data to calculate a schedule.

The essential upgrade over a timer is that the system knows conditions. A timer irrigates during rain; a sensor-linked system does not. That single difference accounts for most of the water saving smart irrigation delivers.

Key points

  • Set thresholds from the soil's field capacity and wilting point, not from a default.
  • Use forecast rainfall to defer irrigation, but verify the forecast's local accuracy first.
  • Zone the system so areas with different soils or crops are controlled separately.
  • Always retain manual override and a maximum run time to limit damage from a stuck valve.
  • Log what was applied and when; an automated system that keeps no record cannot be evaluated.

Example

A vegetable operation links its drip valves to moisture sensors with a threshold set from its own soil data. Water use falls by roughly 35 percent across the season, and the biggest single saving comes from the system simply not running during three days of rain.

Why this matters

Automated irrigation is one of the few AgriTech investments with a directly measurable payback, and it is increasingly affordable at smallholder scale. Understanding thresholds and safeguards is what separates a system that saves water from one that floods a field overnight.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of sensor-linked irrigation over a timer?

questions.question: Why should an automated system have a maximum run time?
options: To limit damage if a valve sticks open

questions.question: Why must an automated system log what it applied?

lessons.title: 7.6 Livestock Monitoring
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Livestock Monitoring
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Livestock Monitoring

Livestock Monitoring is a livestock or aquaculture concept used to support welfare, health, production, records, and responsible management.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Livestock Monitoring
Continuous observation of animals, and what it detects first.

Livestock monitoring uses wearable or fixed devices to observe animals continuously. Collars and ear tags track movement and rumination; scales record weight; cameras and sensors monitor housing conditions; some systems measure body temperature.

The two highest-value applications are oestrus detection and early illness detection. Both work through the same mechanism: activity changes before anything is visible to an observer. A cow in heat moves substantially more; a sick animal ruminates less and moves less, often a day or more before it looks ill.

Key points

  • Missed heats are a major hidden cost in dairy — each one delays calving by roughly three weeks.
  • Rumination time is one of the earliest and most reliable indicators of illness in ruminants.
  • Alerts must reach someone who can act, at a time they can act.
  • Baselines are individual — what is normal activity differs between animals.
  • Monitoring housing conditions (temperature, humidity, ammonia) protects poultry and pigs, where losses are fast.

Example

A collar system flags a cow whose rumination has dropped 20 percent overnight. She looks normal. Examined, she has early mastitis. Treatment starts a day before she would otherwise have been noticed, and she stays in the herd rather than losing a quarter.

Why this matters

Livestock represents stored wealth for many households, and losses are sudden. Monitoring converts an unpredictable loss into an early warning, which is exactly the sort of risk reduction that makes technology worth paying for.

It is easy to measure by eye

lessons.html:

🌱 Greenhouse Automation
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Greenhouse Automation

Greenhouse Automation is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Greenhouse Automation
Controlling a growing environment, and the variables that interact.

A greenhouse lets you control temperature, humidity, light, ventilation, irrigation and sometimes carbon dioxide. Automation manages these continuously through sensors and actuators — vents, fans, screens, heaters, misters and valves.

The complication is that the variables interact. Closing vents to hold temperature raises humidity, which encourages fungal disease. Ventilating to cut humidity loses heat. Good control is a balance rather than a set of independent settings, which is exactly why automation outperforms manual adjustment.

Key points

  • Temperature and humidity must be managed together, never separately.
  • Vapour pressure deficit is a better guide than humidity alone for transpiration and disease risk.
  • Ventilation is the primary tool in hot climates; cooling by other means is expensive.
  • Shade screens reduce heat load and light together — check the crop can spare the light.
  • Every automated greenhouse needs a high-temperature alarm; failures kill a crop within hours.

Example

A grower sets the controller to hold 26°C and closes vents to achieve it during a cool spell. Humidity climbs above 90 percent overnight and botrytis appears within the week. Holding temperature slightly lower with vents partly open would have cost a little growth and saved the crop.

Why this matters

Protected cultivation is expanding in West African horticulture because it extends seasons and protects high-value crops. Understanding the interaction between variables is what prevents an expensive structure from producing disease instead of vegetables.

lessons.title: 7.8 IoT Data Collection
lessons.html:

1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

IoT Data Collection

IoT Data Collection is a digital-agriculture concept used to collect, interpret, communicate, or act on farm information.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 IoT Data Collection
Getting readings off the device and into a usable form.

Collecting IoT data means moving readings from device to storage, and doing so in a form that stays usable. Each reading needs three things attached: which device produced it, when, and what unit it is in. A stream of bare numbers is not data.

Sampling frequency should match how fast the quantity changes. Soil moisture changes over hours, so readings every fifteen minutes are ample. Recording every second fills storage and adds nothing.

Key points

  • Timestamp everything, in a consistent time zone, and say which.
  • Store raw readings; derive averages later rather than storing only summaries.
  • Expect gaps — devices fail and networks drop — and record gaps as gaps, not as zeros.
  • A zero and a missing value mean completely different things; never conflate them.
  • Buffer readings on the device so a network outage delays data rather than losing it.

Example

A dataset shows soil moisture falling to zero for six hours. Investigation shows the network was down and the system wrote zeros for missing readings. Anyone analysing it would conclude the soil dried completely and then instantly rewetted — a physical impossibility caused by a data-handling choice.

Why this matters

Data quality problems introduced at collection cannot be repaired later, and they silently corrupt every analysis built on top. Knowing to insist on timestamps, units and honest gap handling is the difference between a dataset that is useful in three years and one that is not.

options: How fast the measured quantity changes
questions.explanation: Sampling far faster than the quantity changes adds volume without adding information.

lessons.title: 7.9 IoT Farm Management
lessons.html:

2. Measure
3. Decide

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

IoT Farm Management

IoT Farm Management is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 IoT Farm Management
Running a farm on live data without drowning in it.

Once sensors are reporting, the management problem shifts from gathering information to acting on it. The two failure modes are opposite: ignoring the data entirely, and being overwhelmed by it.

The solution to both is management by exception. Rather than reviewing every reading, define the conditions that require action — moisture below a threshold, temperature above a limit, a sensor silent for six hours — and be alerted only when one occurs. Everything else is logged and reviewed periodically, not continuously.

Key points

  • Define thresholds in advance, in writing, with the action each one triggers.
  • Every alert must name what happened, where, and what to do.
  • Too many alerts trains people to ignore all of them — tune thresholds until alerts are rare and real.
  • Include a sensor-silent alert; a dead sensor is itself an exception.
  • Review the full log weekly for trends that never crossed a threshold.

Example

A farm sets fourteen alerts and receives around thirty messages a day. Within a fortnight staff stop reading them, and a genuine tank-empty alert is missed. Reducing to four alerts, each requiring real action, restores attention and the system starts working.

Why this matters

Alert fatigue is the most common reason monitoring systems stop delivering value, and it is a design failure rather than a discipline failure. Being able to design an alerting scheme that people keep using is a practical skill in any monitoring role.

lessons.html:

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

IoT Case Studies

IoT Case Studies is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 IoT Case Studies
What has worked, what has not, and the pattern behind both.

Reviewing real deployments shows a consistent pattern. The successes tend to be narrow: one measurement, one decision, one clear saving. The failures tend to be broad: many sensors, a comprehensive dashboard, and no specific decision that changes.

A second pattern concerns ownership. Systems installed and paid for by the farmer are maintained. Systems installed free by a project are frequently abandoned once the project ends, because nobody has a reason to repair them.

Key points

  • Successful deployments start with one decision worth improving.
  • Payback must be visible to the person paying — ideally within one season.
  • Local repair capability determines whether a system survives its first failure.
  • Shared infrastructure (a cooperative weather station) spreads cost across many users.
  • Ask what happens in year three, not just whether it works in month one.

Example

A cooperative installs one shared weather station and sends a daily spray-risk message to members. Cost per farmer is negligible, the decision it informs is specific, and members can see the fungicide they did not have to buy. Five years later it is still running, unlike three fully-funded sensor networks nearby.

Why this matters

Judging a proposed deployment against these patterns will save you and your employers a great deal of money. The technical question is rarely the one that decides the outcome; ownership, maintenance and decision-focus usually are.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Drone Technology

Drone Technology is a digital-agriculture concept used to collect, interpret, communicate, or act on farm information.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Drone Technology
What agricultural drones are, and the trade-offs between types.

An agricultural drone is an unmanned aircraft carrying a camera or a spray tank. Two types dominate. Multirotor drones take off vertically, hover, and are simple to fly, but their flight time is typically 20 to 30 minutes. Fixed-wing drones fly like aeroplanes, cover much larger areas per flight, but need space to launch and land and cannot hover.

For most farm work below about 50 hectares, a multirotor is the practical choice. The limiting factor is almost always battery endurance, which is why area covered per flight is the specification that matters most.

Key points

  • Flight time falls sharply with payload, wind and temperature — quoted figures are best-case.
  • Carry spare batteries; they are the real determinant of how much you can survey in a day.
  • Camera type sets what you can measure: standard colour for visual inspection, multispectral for vegetation indices.
  • Wind above roughly 8 to 10 metres per second grounds most small drones.
  • Humidity, dust and salt air shorten the life of motors and electronics.

Example

An operator plans to survey 40 hectares with one battery based on the manufacturer's 28-minute figure. In practice, with a multispectral camera fitted and a light wind, flights last 17 minutes and cover about 12 hectares. The job takes four batteries, not one.

Why this matters

Drone services are among the most accessible AgriTech businesses to start, and unrealistic expectations about coverage are the commonest reason early operators lose money on their first contracts.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Agricultural Drone Applications

Agricultural Drone Applications is a digital-agriculture concept used to collect, interpret, communicate, or act on farm information.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Agricultural Drone Applications
What drones are actually used for on farms.

Drone use in agriculture falls into three groups. Mapping produces an orthomosaic — a single geometrically corrected image of a whole field — and from it, plot areas, elevation and drainage patterns. Monitoring uses repeated flights to track crop vigour, spot stress early and assess damage after a storm. Application uses spray drones to apply pesticide or fertiliser, particularly where ground access is difficult.

Mapping and monitoring are where most value sits for smallholder contexts. Spraying requires substantially more regulation, training and capital.

Key points

  • Orthomosaics let you measure areas accurately — often the fastest way to establish plot sizes.
  • Repeat flights on a consistent schedule; change over time is what reveals problems.
  • Damage assessment after flood or storm is fast, and is used for insurance and relief claims.
  • Spray drones suit flooded rice and steep or waterlogged ground where machinery cannot travel.
  • Livestock counting and locating animals in bush is a common, underrated use.

Example

After a windstorm a cooperative flies its 60 hectares in an afternoon and produces a map showing exactly which plots lodged and by how much. The relief claim is submitted with evidence within a week, instead of relying on walk-through estimates that would have taken longer and convinced nobody.

Why this matters

Knowing the range of applications lets you match a drone service to what a client will actually pay for. Mapping for area measurement and damage assessment tend to sell more readily than crop monitoring, because the value is immediate and obvious.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings
