questions.question: What is the usual error in problem solving?
options: Treating a symptom rather than finding the cause
questions.explanation: Responding to the visible symptom leaves the underlying cause in place.

questions.question: Which explanations should be checked first?
options: The cheap and simple ones, such as measurement error or a blockage
questions.explanation: Simple causes are common and quick to rule out, which narrows the search cheaply.

questions.question: Which step is most often omitted?
options: Deciding how you will know whether the response worked
questions.explanation: Without a check, the same problem recurs and nothing is learned from the attempt.

lessons.title: 16.8 Professional Ethics
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Professional Ethics
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Professional Ethics

Professional Ethics is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Professional Ethics
The standards that make your advice worth trusting.

Ethical practice in agriculture matters because the people you advise often cannot verify what you tell them and will commit a season's resources on your word. The imbalance of information creates a duty.

The recurring situations are predictable: being paid a commission to recommend a product, being asked to report results better than they were, discovering an error after a recommendation has been acted on, and being pressed to certify something you have not verified.

Key points

  • Disclose any interest you have in a product you recommend.
  • Report results honestly, including failures; a project that never reports failure is not being measured.
  • Correct your errors promptly and directly to the person affected.
  • Never certify, sign or attest to something you have not verified yourself.
  • Respect the confidentiality of farm data; it belongs to the farmer, not to you.
  • Say plainly when something is outside your competence.

Example

An advisor realises after recommending a planting date that he misread the forecast. Telling the farmer immediately allows part of the planting to be held back. Saying nothing and hoping would have transferred his mistake onto someone else's season.

Why this matters

Your reputation is the asset that determines whether people act on your advice, and in agricultural communities it travels quickly and lasts. Ethical practice is also, practically, what keeps you employable over a career.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Smart Farm Design
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Smart Farm Design
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Smart Farm Design

Smart Farm Design is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Smart Farm Design
Design a complete digital system for one real farm.

Produce a design for how one real farm would be run using the tools in this course. This is a design exercise, not an installation: you are specifying what should exist and why, at a cost the farm could actually meet.

The discipline is to justify every element by the decision it changes. A design that lists equipment without stating what each item changes has not been done.

Key points

  • Describe the farm — size, enterprises, people, current practice and the owner's goal.
  • Identify the three decisions that most affect this farm's results, with evidence.
  • Specify what would inform each — a measurement, a record, or an alert.
  • Choose tools for each, from a notebook upward, with a reason for the choice.
  • Cost it — purchase, running and maintenance, per season.
  • Estimate the return and the payback period.
  • State what could go wrong — power, connectivity, maintenance, skills.
  • Present a one-page diagram and a two-page justification.

Example

A strong design for a two-hectare vegetable farm might specify a plot register and activity log on a phone spreadsheet, one soil moisture probe in the driest bed, a rain gauge read daily, and a weekly WhatsApp price check — total cost under a hundred dollars, with irrigation timing and selling date as the two decisions it changes.

Why this matters

This project demonstrates that you can design proportionately. Recommending inexpensive tools that fit a real farm shows more judgement than specifying equipment the farm could never afford or maintain.

lessons.html:

1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Precision Farming Plan

Precision Farming Plan is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Precision Farming Plan
Produce a zone-based management plan for one field.

Build a full-season precision plan for a single field: what varies within it, how you would divide it, and what you would do differently in each zone.

This extends the Module 6 project across a whole season rather than a single treatment.

Key points

  • Map the field boundary and record its area.
  • Evidence the variation — observation, soil sampling, past yield, or imagery.
  • Define zones with a written justification for each boundary.
  • Plan by operation — land preparation, variety, seed rate, nutrition, protection, irrigation, harvest — stating where treatment differs by zone.
  • Cost the difference against uniform management.
  • Define the measurement — how you will weigh each zone's output separately.
  • Set a decision rule — what result would make you keep, change or abandon the zoning.

Example

A plan might apply a shorter-duration variety and reduced nitrogen on a dry rise, standard treatment mid-slope, and delayed planting with drainage on a wet lower zone — with total input cost held constant and each zone harvested and weighed separately to test it.

Why this matters

Stating in advance what result would change your mind is what distinguishes a plan from an intention, and it is the habit that makes precision agriculture improve over seasons rather than merely being practised.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Digital Farm Record System
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Digital Farm Record System
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Digital Farm Record System

Digital Farm Record System is a digital-agriculture concept used to collect, interpret, communicate, or act on farm information.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Digital Farm Record System
Build and run a record system a real farm will actually maintain.

Design, set up and operate a record system on a real farm for at least four weeks. The test is not the design; it is whether the records are still being kept at the end.

Simplicity is the requirement. A system that captures a little reliably beats one that captures everything for a fortnight and then lapses.

Key points

  • Agree the questions the farm wants answered, with the farmer.
  • Design the fields — the minimum set that answers them.
  • Define the plots and give each a permanent code.
  • Choose the medium — paper, phone spreadsheet or app — based on who records and where.
  • Train whoever records, and watch them do it once.
  • Run it for four weeks, checking weekly.
  • Report — what was captured, what was missed, why, and what you changed.
  • Produce one analysis from the data collected, however small.

Example

An honest submission might report that daily labour recording lapsed within a week because the person doing the work could not stop to write, and that moving to a simple end-of-day tally of hours by plot restored it — a smaller record that survived.

Why this matters

Record systems fail on adoption rather than design, and reporting honestly on what lapsed and how you adapted demonstrates exactly the judgement employers need. This project also produces the data your capstone will analyse.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Irrigation Management Plan
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Irrigation Management Plan
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Irrigation Management Plan

Irrigation Management Plan is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Irrigation Management Plan
Produce a measured irrigation schedule for a real crop.

Build an irrigation plan grounded in measurement rather than habit: what the soil holds, what the crop needs, what the system delivers, and therefore when and how long to run it.

If the farm is rainfed, produce a water conservation and supplementary irrigation plan instead, using the same measurements.

Key points

  • Characterise the soil — texture, and estimated field capacity and wilting point.
  • Measure the system — delivery rate in millimetres per hour over the wetted area.
  • Estimate crop demand across the season, identifying the critical stages.
  • Build the schedule — trigger point, application depth and run time.
  • Plan the monitoring — how soil moisture will be checked and by whom.
  • Cost it — water, fuel or power, labour and maintenance.
  • Compare against current practice and estimate the saving.
  • Include safeguards — maximum run time, leak checks and what to do on failure.

Example

A plan might establish that the system delivers 4mm per hour, that the root zone holds 30mm of usable water, that irrigation should trigger at 50 percent depletion, and therefore that a four-hour run is required — replacing a habitual daily two-hour run that was both insufficient and mistimed.

Why this matters

Converting run time into depth applied is a small calculation almost nobody performs, and it routinely reveals that irrigation is substantially over- or under-applied. This is a concrete, quantified saving to put in a portfolio.

Tap a word to open its definition.

Agribusiness Startup Plan

Agribusiness Startup Plan is an agribusiness concept used to understand customers, costs, income, risk, value, and business decisions.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Agribusiness Startup Plan
Write a complete, fundable plan for one agricultural business.

Produce a full business plan for an agricultural enterprise — production, processing, input supply, services or trading. It may be an existing business or one you intend to start, but it must be real and specific.

The financial section decides it. Projections must rest on figures you can defend.

Key points

  • Summary — what the business does and what it is asking for, in one page.
  • Business model — the offer, the customer, the channel and why they choose you.
  • Market evidence — recorded prices, buyer conversations, or a commitment.
  • Operations — the production or service plan with a calendar.
  • Financials — gross margins, monthly cash flow, the maximum deficit, and break-even.
  • Funding — how much, for what, and how it will be repaid.
  • Risks — the three largest, each with a response.
  • Evidence annex — the price records and quotes behind your numbers.

Example

A strong plan states a break-even yield, identifies the maximum cash deficit and the month it occurs, and attaches four weeks of recorded market prices plus a signed expression of interest from one buyer — so every projection can be traced to something observed.

Why this matters

This is the document through which agricultural finance is actually accessed, and being able to produce one is a service you can sell immediately to farmers and cooperatives who cannot.

Farm Marketing Campaign

Farm Marketing Campaign is a digital-agriculture concept used to collect, interpret, communicate, or act on farm information.

📖 Farm Marketing Campaign
Run and measure a second campaign, applying what the first taught.

Design, run and evaluate a marketing campaign for a real agricultural product. If you completed the Module 11 project, this one must apply a lesson from it and say explicitly what changed.

Measurement against a stated objective is the requirement.

Key points

  • State the lesson you are applying from previous marketing work.
  • Define product, buyer and objective — the objective as a number.
  • Set a budget, including your own time valued honestly.
  • Choose channels with a reason for each.
  • Produce the material with one clear call to action.
  • Run for a defined period, recording responses as they occur.
  • Measure — enquiries, orders, revenue, cost per order.
  • Compare against the previous campaign and explain the difference.

Example

A submission might report that narrowing the delivery radius from city-wide to three kilometres cut enquiries by half but raised completed orders, because the earlier campaign generated interest from people who could not be served — a clear, measured improvement in cost per order.

Why this matters

Demonstrating that you changed an approach based on measured evidence, and that the change worked, is more persuasive to an employer than any single successful campaign.

lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Climate-Smart Agriculture Project
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Climate-Smart Agriculture Project

Climate-Smart Agriculture Project is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Climate-Smart Agriculture Project
Design and begin a practice that raises productivity, resilience and carbon together.

Select one climate-smart practice, justify it for a specific farm, implement at least part of it, and set up the measurement that will show whether it worked.

The practice must be assessed against all three objectives, and against the worst season it will face rather than the average.

Key points

  • Assess the farm's climate risk — what has changed, with evidence from records or from the farmer.
  • Select a practice and justify it against productivity, resilience and mitigation.
  • Check adoption barriers — labour timing, cash, land tenure, acceptability.
  • Implement on at least part of the farm, leaving an untreated comparison.
  • Measure — define what you will record and how often.
  • Cost it, including labour, and state the payback expected.
  • Report what was done, what was observed so far, and what remains to be seen.

Example

A project might establish mulching and tied ridges on half a plot with the other half unchanged, record soil moisture weekly at both, and report after six weeks that the treated half retained moisture measurably longer through a dry spell — while noting that the yield effect cannot yet be known.

Why this matters

Leaving an untreated comparison is what makes the result evidence rather than an impression, and stating plainly what cannot yet be concluded is what makes the report trustworthy.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Data Analytics Project
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Data Analytics Project
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Data Analytics Project

Data Analytics Project is a digital-agriculture concept used to collect, interpret, communicate, or act on farm information.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Data Analytics Project
Analyse a multi-farm or multi-season dataset and report the findings.

Where the Module 9 project analysed one farm's records, this one works with a larger dataset: several farms, or several seasons from one farm. The analytical question is comparison across units, and the new difficulty is that the units differ in more ways than the one you care about.

If no dataset is available, combine records from three farms you can access, and say clearly how they were assembled.

Key points

  • Assemble — one flat table, consistent units, a clear identifier per farm and season.
  • Document the cleaning — every correction and every record excluded, with the reason.
  • Describe the data — how many farms, seasons, plots and observations.
  • Compute yield, cost and margin per unit for each.
  • Compare and identify the largest differences.
  • Test explanations against the data rather than assuming the obvious one.
  • Address confounding — state what else differs between the units you compared.
  • Visualise and recommend, stating your confidence honestly.

Example

A strong submission might find that the highest-yielding farms are also those nearest the road, note that this could reflect either better input access or better soil rather than management, and state that the data cannot separate the two — which is a more useful finding than a confident wrong attribution.

Why this matters

Recognising confounding and saying what the data cannot establish is the analytical judgement that separates a trustworthy analyst from someone who produces charts. It is also what donors and employers most often find missing.

lessons.html:

🌱 Community Agriculture Initiative
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Community Agriculture Initiative

Community Agriculture Initiative is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Community Agriculture Initiative
Design an intervention that a group will actually adopt and sustain.

Design an initiative benefiting a group of farmers — shared equipment, a collective input purchase, a demonstration plot, a group storage facility, a shared weather station and advisory message.

The design must address sustainability explicitly: what happens when the initial support ends. This is where most community projects fail.

Key points

  • Identify the shared problem through conversation, not assumption.
  • Confirm it matters — evidence that the group considers it a priority.
  • Design the intervention and state who does what.
  • Governance — who decides, who holds funds, how disputes are settled.
  • Cost and contribution — what members contribute; free provision undermines ownership.
  • Sustainability plan — maintenance, replacement and who pays, after year one.
  • Inclusion — how women and poorer households can participate in practice.
  • Measurement — what would show it worked.

Example

A shared thresher initiative might charge a per-bag fee that covers fuel, maintenance and a replacement fund, with a written rota, a treasurer separate from the operator, and published accounts — so it continues after the organisation that helped establish it has left.

Why this matters

The sustainability and governance sections are what distinguish a project that lasts from one that runs while funded. Being able to design those is what community-facing agricultural roles actually require.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Agricultural Innovation Pitch
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Agricultural Innovation Pitch
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Agricultural Innovation Pitch

Agricultural Innovation Pitch is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Agricultural Innovation Pitch
Present an idea persuasively and answer hard questions about it.

Prepare and deliver a short pitch for an agricultural innovation — a product, a service or a business. It must be a real idea you could pursue, and it must survive scrutiny.

A pitch is not a description. It must convince a listener that the problem is real, the solution works, someone will pay, and you can deliver it.

Key points

  • The problem — whose problem, how big, and what it costs them today.
  • The solution — what it is, in plain language, in two sentences.
  • Evidence — what you have tested and what you learned.
  • The market — who pays, how much, and how you know.
  • The model — how the money works.
  • Why you — what you specifically bring.
  • The ask — exactly what you need.
  • Prepare for the hard questions — why hasn't someone done this, what if the assumption is wrong, what is the riskiest part.

Example

A strong pitch opens by stating that farmers in one district lose a measured share of their maize to storage mould, names what that costs them, and describes a tested drying and storage service with the results of a small trial — rather than opening with a description of the technology.

Why this matters

Pitching is how funding, partnerships and jobs are obtained. Preparing for the hard questions in advance is what allows you to answer them calmly, and the answers are usually more persuasive than the pitch itself.

lessons.title: 18.1 Building an AgriTech Portfolio
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Building an AgriTech Portfolio
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Building an AgriTech Portfolio

Building an AgriTech Portfolio is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Building an AgriTech Portfolio
Assembling evidence that you can do the work.

A portfolio is the collection of work you can show. In AgriTech it matters more than a certificate, because employers have learned that a certificate says what you were taught while a portfolio shows what you produced.

Everything in this course has been building it: the zone map, the drone survey report, the record system, the data analysis, the business plan, the marketing campaign. What remains is to present them so a stranger can see the quality quickly.

Key points

  • Lead with the two strongest pieces; a reviewer may not reach the third.
  • For each piece state the problem, what you did, what you found, and what changed as a result.
  • Include the honest limitations; they demonstrate judgement rather than weakness.
  • Use real data from real farms, anonymised if the farmer prefers.
  • Keep it accessible — a PDF and a folder of files, not a platform an employer must join.
  • One page per piece is usually enough; attach the full document beneath.

Example

A portfolio opens with a two-page summary of a farm analysis showing that reallocating labour raised margin per labour day by a measured amount, with the chart that demonstrates it. The full workbook is attached. A reviewer understands the candidate's ability in ninety seconds.

Why this matters

This is the single most useful thing you take from the course, and it is the item that most often decides an interview. It also works for freelance and consulting clients, who want evidence rather than qualifications.

lessons.title: 18.2 Resume Writing
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Resume Writing
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Resume Writing

Resume Writing is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Resume Writing
A document that gets you to an interview.

A resume exists to secure an interview, not to describe your life. It is read quickly, often against a list of requirements, so it must make the match visible immediately.

The recurring weakness is listing duties rather than results. Responsible for data collection says nothing. Designed and ran a record system across 40 farms; identified a 30 percent gap in input cost per hectare between plots says what you can do.

Key points

  • Keep it to one or two pages, with the most relevant material first.
  • Write results with numbers: how many, how much, what changed.
  • Mirror the language of the advertisement where it honestly applies.
  • List concrete tools you can actually use — spreadsheets, QGIS, specific record systems.
  • Include the portfolio link or note that samples are available.
  • Remove anything that does not support the application.

Example

Two candidates list the same course. One writes trained in agricultural data analysis. The other writes analysed three seasons of records across 12 plots; found that the highest-yielding plot had the lowest margin due to transport cost; recommended a change adopted by the farm. Only the second demonstrates capability.

Why this matters

Most applications are rejected at the resume stage, usually because the match to the requirements is not visible. Writing results rather than duties is the change that most improves the response rate.

📖 LinkedIn Optimization
Being findable by people who are looking for your skills.

LinkedIn functions as a searchable directory of professionals. Recruiters and organisations search it by keyword, so appearing in the right searches depends on the words in your headline, your summary and your experience.

For agricultural roles the useful keywords are specific and practical: agronomy, farm data, GIS, QGIS, monitoring and evaluation, value chain, extension, precision agriculture, agribusiness. Generic phrases about being hardworking match nothing anyone searches for.

Key points

  • Put your actual skills in the headline, not just a job title.
  • Write the summary in the first person and state what you do and for whom.
  • Describe roles with results, exactly as in a resume.
  • List concrete tools; recruiters search for them by name.
  • Share your project work — a short post about a farm analysis demonstrates ability publicly.
  • Connect with people in the sector; visibility follows from activity.

Example

A graduate changes her headline from Recent graduate seeking opportunities to Farm data and GIS — record systems, yield analysis, QGIS mapping for smallholder agriculture. She begins appearing in searches for GIS and farm data, and receives enquiries she was previously invisible to.

Why this matters

A large share of agricultural sector recruitment now begins with a keyword search, and being absent from the results is indistinguishable from not existing. This is a small amount of work with a disproportionate effect.

lessons.title: 18.4 Interview Preparation
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Interview Preparation
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Interview Preparation

Interview Preparation is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Interview Preparation
Answering well by preparing evidence, not scripts.

Interviews test three things: whether you can do the work, whether you will fit the team, and whether you understand the context. Most questions are variants of tell me about a time when, and they are answered with specific examples rather than general claims.

A workable structure is to describe the situation briefly, the task, what you specifically did, and the result with a number. Preparing five such examples covers most of what you will be asked, because the same experiences can answer many different questions.

Key points

  • Prepare five concrete examples from your project work, each with a measurable result.
  • Research the organisation: what they do, where, and what they are currently working on.
  • Prepare questions of your own; having none suggests you are not evaluating them.
  • Say plainly when you do not know something, and say how you would find out.
  • Bring your portfolio and offer it; showing beats describing.
  • Expect a practical question — a farmer's problem, or a dataset to interpret.

Example

Asked to describe a difficult problem, a candidate explains that a record system lapsed within a week, that she found the cause was the recorder not being able to stop mid-task, and that a simplified end-of-day tally restored it. The honesty about the initial failure makes the recovery credible.

Why this matters

Interviews are where preparation is most visible and most rewarded. Having examples ready means you spend the interview demonstrating rather than searching your memory.

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Freelancing Opportunities

Freelancing Opportunities is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Freelancing Opportunities
Selling specific services independently.

Freelancing means selling a defined service for a fee rather than taking employment. In AgriTech the services that sell are concrete and bounded: drone mapping, farm record system setup, data analysis and reporting, proposal writing, business plan preparation, and GIS mapping.

The difficulty is not delivering the work but finding clients and getting paid. Both are addressed by starting with people who already know you, doing one job well, and asking for an introduction.

Key points

  • Offer a specific, bounded service — not general assistance.
  • Price by the job rather than by the hour where the scope is clear.
  • Put the scope in writing: what is included, what is not, and what happens if it changes.
  • Take a deposit; it filters out clients who were never going to pay.
  • Deliver something visible early, so the client sees progress.
  • Ask every satisfied client for one introduction.

Example

A graduate offers a fixed-price service: map a farm, set up a plot register and produce a one-page yield and cost summary, for an agreed fee within two weeks. It is easy to explain, easy to price, and easy for a cooperative to approve.

Why this matters

Freelancing is a realistic route to income while building experience, and in many places it is more available than formal employment. A bounded, clearly priced service is far easier to sell than open-ended availability.

1. Observe

4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Consulting Opportunities

Consulting Opportunities is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Consulting Opportunities
Advising organisations, and what they are actually buying.

Consulting differs from freelancing in what is sold. A freelancer delivers a task; a consultant delivers judgement — an assessment, a recommendation, a decision the client could not confidently make alone.

Clients in agriculture include NGOs, donor programmes, cooperatives, processors, input companies and banks lending to agriculture. What they buy is reduced uncertainty, so credibility is the product. It rests on relevant experience, honest reporting, and being willing to deliver findings the client did not want.

Key points

  • Define the question precisely before agreeing the work; vague terms of reference cause disputes.
  • Agree the deliverable, the timeline and the payment schedule in writing.
  • Gather your own evidence rather than relying on what the client provides.
  • Report what you found, including findings that are unwelcome.
  • State the limits of your evidence explicitly.
  • Your independence is the asset; a consultant who tells clients what they want becomes worthless.

Example

A consultant assessing a proposed processing facility finds that local supply cannot fill it for eight months of the year. Reporting that plainly saves the client a substantial investment and earns further work, even though it was not the answer they hoped for.

Why this matters

Consulting is where experienced agricultural professionals earn most, and it is built on a reputation for honest assessment. Protecting that independence from the beginning is what makes the career possible.

📖 Professional Certifications
Credentials that carry weight, and when they are worth pursuing.

Certifications relevant to AgriTech careers include GlobalGAP internal auditor training, food safety qualifications such as HACCP, GIS certifications, project management credentials, monitoring and evaluation training, and drone operator licensing.

A certification is worth pursuing when it is a stated requirement for roles you want, when it grants a legal permission you need, or when it teaches something you genuinely lack. It is not worth pursuing to appear more qualified in general; employers in this sector weigh demonstrated work more heavily.

Key points

  • Check job advertisements for the roles you want and see what is actually required.
  • Prioritise certifications that grant a permission, such as drone operation.
  • Compare the cost and time against the wage difference it unlocks.
  • A certification with practical assessment carries more weight than one with an examination only.
  • Keep evidence of the work you did during the certification; that is what you will show.

Example

A candidate considering two courses checks twenty relevant advertisements. GIS appears in eleven; a general agribusiness certificate appears in none. The choice is settled by evidence rather than by which sounds more impressive.

Why this matters

Certifications cost money and time that could go into portfolio work, so the decision deserves evidence. Checking actual advertisements is a simple method that most people skip.

Career Growth Plan

Career Growth Plan is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Career Growth Plan
Deciding where you are going and what to do next.

A career plan states where you want to be, what that requires, and what you will do in the next twelve months. Without one, careers drift towards whatever opportunity appears, which is not always the direction you would have chosen.

The useful form is short and concrete: a destination two to three years out, the three capabilities it requires, an honest assessment of where you stand on each, and one action per gap with a date.

Key points

  • State a destination specific enough to plan towards — a type of role, not simply advancement.
  • Identify the three capabilities it requires, from real job advertisements.
  • Assess yourself honestly against each, using evidence from your portfolio.
  • Set one concrete action per gap, with a date.
  • Review every six months; destinations change as you learn what the work is actually like.
  • Keep building the portfolio throughout; it is the currency of every step.

Example

A plan might state: within three years, monitoring and evaluation officer for an agricultural programme. Requirements: data analysis, M&E methodology, report writing. Gaps: M&E methodology. Action: complete an M&E course by June and apply it to a real project, documented for the portfolio.

Why this matters

This is the last lesson of the course because it points at what happens afterwards. The habit of assessing yourself against real requirements, and closing one gap at a time with documented work, is what turns a certificate into a career.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Identify an Agricultural Challenge
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Identify an Agricultural Challenge
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Identify an Agricultural Challenge

Identify an Agricultural Challenge is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Identify an Agricultural Challenge
Choose the problem your capstone will address, and prove it is real.

The capstone begins by selecting one specific problem on one real farm or in one real farming community. Everything that follows depends on this choice, and the commonest capstone failure is a problem chosen because it is interesting rather than because it is real.

A well-chosen problem is narrow, observable and costly to the person who has it. Low productivity is not a problem statement; it is a category. Plot C yields a third less than the others every season is a problem you can investigate.

Key points

  • Choose the farm or community — one you can visit repeatedly, not one you have heard about.
  • Listen first — ask what the farmer considers their biggest difficulty, before deciding.
  • State the problem in observable terms: what happens, where, how often, and to what extent.
  • Quantify the cost — in yield, money, labour or risk. A problem with no cost is not worth solving.
  • Check it is tractable — can you investigate it with the time and access you have?
  • Confirm with the farmer that this is a problem they want solved.
  • Write one page: the problem, its cost, why it matters, and how you will know it is solved.

Example

A weak statement reads the farm needs to modernise. A strong one reads roughly 30 percent of the maize harvest is lost to mould in storage each year, costing around $260, because the crop is bagged before it is dry enough and stored on a bare floor. The second can be investigated, measured and resolved.

Why this matters

Choosing the problem well determines whether the remaining seven stages produce anything useful. A vague problem yields a vague capstone; a specific, costed one produces work an employer can immediately understand.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Conduct Farm Research
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Conduct Farm Research
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Conduct Farm Research

Conduct Farm Research is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Conduct Farm Research
Gather the evidence that establishes what is actually happening.

Research here means systematic observation rather than literature review. You are establishing the facts of the situation: measurements, records, conditions and what the people involved say.

The discipline is to gather evidence before forming a conclusion. It is easy to arrive with an explanation already in mind and collect only what confirms it, which produces a confident and wrong capstone.

Key points

  • Plan what to collect — list the measurements and records that would distinguish between possible causes.
  • Map the site — plot boundaries, areas and relevant features, with GPS positions.
  • Measure — soil, moisture, yields, weights, costs, times, whatever the problem requires.
  • Interview — the farmer, workers and anyone else involved, recording what they say rather than your interpretation.
  • Photograph with positions and dates.
  • Record conditions — rainfall, timing, anything that could confound the comparison.
  • List the possible causes and note which evidence supports or contradicts each.
  • State what you could not establish and why.

Example

Investigating the storage losses, you measure grain moisture at bagging on three occasions, record store conditions, weigh a sample of bags at bagging and again after eight weeks, and photograph the mould distribution within the stack. The evidence points to moisture at bagging rather than to the store itself.

Why this matters

This stage produces the evidence base for everything after it. Listing several possible causes before investigating, and recording what contradicts your favoured explanation, is what makes the conclusion trustworthy.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Design a Digital Agriculture Solution
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Design a Digital Agriculture Solution
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Design a Digital Agriculture Solution

Design a Digital Agriculture Solution is a digital-agriculture concept used to collect, interpret, communicate, or act on farm information.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Design a Digital Agriculture Solution
Specify what should change, and justify every element.

With the cause established, design the response. It will usually combine a measurement, a record and a changed practice, and it must be proportionate to the farm's means.

Every element must be justified by the evidence you gathered and by the decision it changes. A design that includes a sensor because sensors are modern has failed, however well presented.

Key points

  • State the cause your research established, with the evidence for it.
  • Specify the response — what will be measured, recorded, and done differently.
  • Justify each element against the evidence and the decision it changes.
  • Choose the simplest tool that does the job; start from a notebook and move up only with reason.
  • Check feasibility — cost, skills, power, connectivity, maintenance and who operates it.
  • Design the records that will show whether it worked.
  • Identify failure modes — what would make this stop working, and what happens then.
  • Produce a one-page diagram and a short written justification.

Example

For the storage problem the design might be a moisture meter shared between four farmers, a simple drying protocol with a recorded moisture reading before bagging, pallets to lift bags off the floor, and a monthly inspection log — with total cost, who holds the meter, and what happens if it breaks.

Why this matters

Designing proportionately is the judgement employers most want to see. A cheap, maintainable solution matched to the evidence demonstrates more capability than an elaborate one the farm could never sustain.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Develop an Agribusiness Plan
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Develop an Agribusiness Plan
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Develop an Agribusiness Plan

Develop an Agribusiness Plan is an agribusiness concept used to understand customers, costs, income, risk, value, and business decisions.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Develop an Agribusiness Plan
Show that the solution makes commercial sense.

A solution that works agronomically but loses money will not be adopted, and should not be. This stage establishes whether the change pays and how it would be funded.

Use the tools from Modules 5, 10 and 13: gross margin, cash flow, break-even and payback. Base every figure on what you measured rather than on what is typical elsewhere.

Key points

  • Cost the solution — purchase, installation, running cost, maintenance and labour.
  • Quantify the benefit — the loss avoided or the gain achieved, from your own measurements.
  • Compute payback and state the assumptions behind it.
  • Build the cash flow by month, and identify the maximum deficit.
  • Identify funding — own resources, input credit, a loan, a group purchase, or a grant.
  • Test the downside — what if the benefit is half what you expect?
  • Name the risks and state a response for each.
  • State plainly whether you would recommend proceeding.

Example

The storage solution costs $85 shared across four farmers, or roughly $21 each, against a measured annual loss of about $260 per farm. Payback is well under one season even if the loss is only halved, and the shared purchase removes the need for credit entirely.

Why this matters

Being willing to conclude that a solution does not pay is as valuable as recommending one that does. A capstone that honestly recommends against its own proposal, with the figures to support it, demonstrates real judgement.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Present a Precision Farming Strategy
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Present a Precision Farming Strategy
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Present a Precision Farming Strategy

Present a Precision Farming Strategy is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Present a Precision Farming Strategy
Set out how the farm would be managed with variation in mind.

Beyond the specific problem, present a strategy for managing the farm's variation over the coming seasons: zones, differentiated treatment, monitoring and the loop that refines them.

This is where the capstone moves from fixing one problem to improving how the farm is run. It should be realistic about what the farm can sustain.

Key points

  • Present the farm map with zones and the evidence behind each boundary.
  • State what differs between zones — soil, drainage, distance, past yield.
  • Plan differentiated management by operation, naming which inputs vary and by how much.
  • Specify monitoring — what is measured, how often, by whom.
  • Define the feedback loop — how this season's results update next season's zones.
  • Phase it — what to do in year one, year two and year three.
  • Set decision rules — what result would cause you to change or abandon the approach.
  • Keep it affordable and state the annual cost.

Example

A three-year phasing might begin with weighing each zone's harvest separately and recording inputs by zone, add differentiated fertiliser rates in year two once two seasons of data exist, and consider a shared moisture meter in year three only if the records justify it.

Why this matters

Phasing demonstrates that you understand adoption. A strategy that asks a farm to change everything at once will be abandoned; one that starts with measurement and earns each subsequent step is one that might actually be followed.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Prepare a Budget
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Prepare a Budget
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Prepare a Budget

Prepare a Budget is an agribusiness concept used to understand customers, costs, income, risk, value, and business decisions.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Prepare a Budget
Set out the full financial picture in a form someone can check.

Bring the numbers together into a complete budget: what the farm currently earns and spends, what the proposed changes cost, and what the position becomes if they are adopted.

Every figure must be traceable to something you measured or a quote you obtained. A budget with unsourced numbers cannot be checked, and an uncheckable budget is not evidence.

Key points

  • Current position — gross margin by enterprise, fixed costs, and net farm income.
  • Cost of the changes — itemised, with the source of each figure.
  • Projected position after adoption, with the assumptions stated.
  • Monthly cash flow for the coming year, showing the maximum deficit.
  • Break-even — the yield or price at which the enterprise stops paying.
  • Sensitivity — the position if yield or price is 20 percent worse.
  • Funding requirement and how it would be met.
  • Source note for every figure: measured, quoted, or estimated with a reason.

Example

A budget line reading drying labour $18 (6 days × $3, measured over two batches in August) can be checked and challenged. A line reading drying labour $18 cannot, and a reader has no way to judge whether it is credible.

Why this matters

Traceable figures are what make a budget persuasive to a lender or an employer. Sourcing every line is a small discipline that separates work that will be trusted from work that will be questioned.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Final Presentation
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Final Presentation
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Final Presentation

Final Presentation is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Final Presentation
Communicate the whole project clearly to someone who was not there.

Present the capstone as a coherent piece of work: the problem, the evidence, the solution, the economics and the recommendation. Your audience knows nothing about the farm, so the presentation must carry them from nothing to a conclusion.

Lead with the finding, not the process. An audience that knows the conclusion in the first minute can follow the evidence; one that must wait for it stops paying attention.

Key points

  • Open with the conclusion — the problem, its cost, and what you recommend.
  • Establish the context briefly — the farm, its scale and its situation.
  • Show the evidence — two or three charts or images that carry the argument.
  • Explain the solution and why each element is there.
  • Give the economics — cost, benefit, payback, in plain numbers.
  • State the limitations — what you could not establish.
  • Close with the recommendation and what happens next.
  • Prepare for questions — especially about your evidence and your assumptions.

Example

A presentation opens: this farm loses about $260 of maize a year to storage mould; the cause is bagging before the grain is dry; a shared $85 moisture meter and a recorded drying protocol would recover most of it within one season. Everything after that is the evidence for those three sentences.

Why this matters

This is the portfolio piece most likely to be seen by an employer, and clarity is what makes it work. Leading with the conclusion is the single change that most improves a technical presentation.

lessons.title: 🛠️ Project Evaluation
lessons.html:
Smart farming cycle
🌱 Project Evaluation
1. Observe
2. Measure
3. Decide
4. Improve

🔑 Key Words & Meanings

Tap a word to open its definition.

Project Evaluation

Project Evaluation is an AgriTech concept or practice used to improve agricultural decisions, productivity, resilience, safety, or market value.

field evidence

measurements, observations, records, photographs, samples, or verified reports used to support an agricultural conclusion

agronomy

the science and practice of managing soil and crops for productive, sustainable agriculture

farm decision

a choice about production, resources, timing, risk, markets, or technology based on goals and evidence

📖 Project Evaluation
Assess your own work honestly, including what it got wrong.

The final stage evaluates the capstone itself: what you set out to do, what you achieved, what you would do differently, and what remains unknown.

Honest self-assessment is the hardest and most valuable part. A capstone claiming complete success is less credible than one identifying its own weaknesses, because every real project has some.

Key points

  • Restate the objective and assess plainly whether it was met.
  • Assess the evidence — how strong was it, and what would have made it stronger?
  • Identify what you got wrong — a wrong initial assumption, a measurement you should have taken.
  • Separate what you controlled from what you did not.
  • State what remains unknown and what would be needed to establish it.
  • Describe what you would do differently with the same time again.
  • Name what you learned — specifically, not generally.
  • Set out the next step for the farm, and for you.

Example

A strong evaluation might record that the initial assumption was a faulty store, that two weeks were spent examining the building before moisture was measured, that measuring at bagging first would have found the cause much sooner, and that one season cannot confirm the fix will hold across a wetter year.

Why this matters

This section is what marks the difference between a student and a professional. Identifying your own errors and stating what your evidence cannot support is exactly the judgement that makes someone worth employing.
